records.name_note: Punica granatum is treated as the correct/accepted name (RHS Name Status: Correct). NC State lists Granatum punicum and Punica nana as names the species was previously known as. Family placement differs across admissible sources: NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden and RHS place it in Lythraceae (the henna family), while UF/IFAS lists the family as Punicaceae.
records.cool_rest_note: Deciduous, with a winter rest. Missouri Botanical Garden (container culture where not hardy): "Plants must be overwintered indoors in bright, cool locations with reduced watering and may defoliate." RHS: "Water sparingly in winter." UGA: most varieties do not require winter chill hours, but all varieties benefit from a rest period or dormancy, and a minimum chill-hour requirement cannot currently be assigned. Cold tolerance depends on dormancy state: UF/IFAS documents late-freeze damage at 28°F to a non-dormant tree versus severe injury at 12°F for dormant trees, so a plant still in leaf (indoors, or in a warm autumn) should be protected at temperatures well above the dormant-tree threshold.
records.water_dry_down_target: Missouri Botanical Garden: "Allow the soil to dry out almost completely before watering thoroughly." Fruit-growing sources (Clemson, UGA, UF/IFAS) add that even, adequate moisture during growth reduces fruit drop and splitting, so a fruiting plant should not be allowed to swing between bone-dry and soaked; see unknowns.
records.water_estimate_basis: UF/IFAS states that in-ground trees "should be irrigated every 7‒10 days in the absence of significant rainfall"; the lower bound (7 days) is taken as the growing-season check interval. This is Florida orchard/dooryard in-ground guidance, not a container figure: a container plant in full sun will dry faster, and Missouri Botanical Garden's regime is to let the soil dry almost completely before watering thoroughly, so treat 7 days as a check cadence rather than a fixed schedule.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: left null. None of the admissible sources address toxicity of Punica granatum to cats, dogs, or any animal; NC State's profile carries no poison section and RHS's profile has no 'Potentially harmful' field. Every source treats the fruit (arils) as edible. Nothing was inferred.

chill_damage_f 12: taken as the dormant-tree damage-onset figure. UF/IFAS: temperatures down to 12°F 'may severely injure dormant trees'; UGA: 'Most pomegranate cultivars are hardy down to 12 degrees F, with the hardier types surviving without damage down to 7 degrees F.' The lower kill-to-ground survival threshold ('killed to the ground at temperatures below 10° F' per NC State; Clemson gives the same 10°F figure for Zone 7b) was deliberately NOT used per the survival-vs-damage-onset rule. Important caveat: UF/IFAS says non-dormant trees are damaged at higher temperatures and documents 'Late freeze damage (28°F) to a non-dormant tree'; a container plant kept in leaf should be treated as non-dormant and protected at or before ~28°F. RHS rates it H3 ('hardy in coastal and relatively mild parts of the UK (-5 to 1)' °C). Clemson notes the 'Russian series' cultivars are hardier (to USDA Zone 6) and that cold-damaged plants usually re-sprout from the crown.

day_f_min / day_f_max / night_f_min / night_f_max: left null. No admissible source gives a day/night growing-temperature range. Related but non-mappable statements: UGA says plants 'perform best when temperatures are above 85 degrees F for at least 120 days a year'; MoBot says species plants need 'high temperatures (90°F+)' to fruit; UF/IFAS says best fruit comes from 'cool winters and hot, dry summers'; RHS says fruit ripening 'Requires high autumn temperatures (13-16°C)'.

humidity_need low is derived from fruit-set and climate statements, not an ambient RH figure: UGA 'Flowers may not set or will abort if conditions are too humid' and flowers 'are highly sensitive to humidity and moisture'; MoBot 'require dry, somewhat arid conditions'; NC State and Clemson both say plants fruit poorly in the humid Southeast. The plant itself grows and flowers well in humid South Carolina (Clemson); low humidity matters mainly for fruit set and disease (leaf/fruit spots, anthracnose). humidity_pct_min/max: no admissible source gives percentages.

light_fc_min / light_fc_good / direct_sun_hours_max: left null. Sources state a minimum, not a maximum: NC State tags full sun '(6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and UGA requires 'at least six hours of direct sunlight a day' for fruit color and productivity; no source caps sun hours or gives foot-candles. The only shading advice is RHS's under-glass instruction 'in full light with shade from hot sun', which is greenhouse-specific. UGA notes fruit sunscald/sunburn can occur but calls it a small percentage of fruit.

soil_drainage: left null on a genuine cross-source conflict rather than picked. NC State's structured Soil Drainage tags are 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist' (its prose: 'good drainage and moisture'), which under the mechanical tag rule would map to moisture_retentive; but UF/IFAS says optimum growth is on 'well-drained, not heavy or moist soils', MoBot specifies 'dry to medium moisture, well-drained' loams, and UGA says trees 'prefer well-drained soils' and 'Extended periods of excessive moisture will harm the trees' -- while both UGA ('can tolerate short periods of standing water') and UF/IFAS ('tolerant of some flooding') describe brief wet tolerance, which rules out 'fast'. NC State's own problems list includes 'root rot may occur'. No single enum token is supported without picking a side.

soil_base garden_bed: chosen as the primary, most-supported growing context (UGA: 'deep loamy soils', also sandy and clay; UF/IFAS: 'deep, loams', adapted 'from pure sand to heavy clay'; NC State: 'all types of soil'). No schema token distinguishes outdoor/greenhouse container culture. For containers, RHS specifies 'peat-free, loam-based compost' under glass, MoBot 'a rich fertile soil mix', and Clemson says 'The compact forms perform quite well in large containers.'

soil_ph_min 5.5 / soil_ph_max 7.0 follow Clemson ('pH 5.5 – 7.0') and UF/IFAS ('pH range of 5.5‒7.0'). UGA gives a slightly wider 5.5 to 7.2 and calls trees 'tolerant of moderately acid to slightly alkaline soils'; UF/IFAS adds 'Growth on alkaline soils is poor.' NC State and RHS tag acid, neutral and alkaline tolerance without numbers.

water_regime dry_thoroughly_between rests on MoBot's explicit instruction ('Allow the soil to dry out almost completely before watering thoroughly'), the only admissible statement that maps directly to an enum; every source calls the plant drought tolerant once established. Fruit-growing sources emphasize steadier moisture during growth: Clemson 'Maintain even soil moisture to reduce fruit drop and splitting'; UGA 'ensuring adequate soil moisture will result in a substantial improvement in plant vigor and fruit yield'; UF/IFAS warns 'Sudden changes in irrigation amounts and timing often lead to fruit splitting' and recommends gradually reducing irrigation as fruit matures; RHS (under glass) says 'During growth, water freely'. UF/IFAS and UGA also warn that excess irrigation/over-fertilization aggravates fruit drop on young trees. For a plant grown for fruit, err toward the 'even moisture' end of this regime.

water_dormant_days_est / water_check_depth_cm: left null. RHS says 'Water sparingly in winter' and MoBot 'reduced watering' for overwintered containers, but no source gives a dormant-season day interval or a soil-probe depth.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_strength: left null. RHS's 'balanced liquid fertiliser monthly' is a word-based cadence with no dilution strength; UGA's schedule is 'three times a year (early spring, late spring and summer)' -- season names only -- at a per-foot-of-height rate ('1 ounce of 10-10-10 per foot of bush height'), and Clemson's is a per-height rate ('1 lb. (one pound) 10-10-10 per 3 ft. of plant height'), neither of which is a dilution fraction. fertilize_active_months [3, 7] comes from Clemson's literal 'Fertilize in March and July'. UGA cautions that 'excessive nitrogen in the late summer to early fall' hurts fruit color and size and 'may also increase the susceptibility of the tree to early chilling temperatures'; UF/IFAS says over-fertilization aggravates fruit drop.

is_houseplant false applies to the species: MoBot says 'Species plants generally do not perform well as indoor plants', but that the dwarf 'Nana' 'may perform well in a sunny window' and 'is considered to be a much better alternative for indoor use'. Indoor use in the sources is otherwise winter protection only: NC State suggests 'a container that can be brought indoors for the winter' and MoBot says 'Where not winter hardy, grow in containers which are overwintered indoors.' RHS lists it under Conservatory Greenhouse and gives under-glass culture.

Fruit-set notes (decision-relevant, no schema field): UGA says 'Pomegranates are self-fruitful', but Clemson recommends 'Plant two or more pomegranate plants, as cross-pollination increases fruit set.' Clemson lists inadequate sunlight, lack of pollination, and over-pruning or cold damage as the usual reasons for no fruit; plants flower on new growth, and heavy pruning reduces fruiting. MoBot says species plants 'will not produce any fruit' in climates like St. Louis; NC State and Clemson say fruiting is unreliable in the humid Southeast. Double-flowered ornamental cultivars produce few or no fruit (Clemson).

records.name_note: NC State lists Olea sativa as a former name for this species.
records.cool_rest_note: Needs a cool winter rest to flower: NC State says 2 months at 40 to 50 F; Missouri Botanical Garden says at least two months below 50 F and to overwinter indoor containers in cool 40-50 F conditions; UF/IFAS says flowering initiation is driven by winter chilling that removes dormancy.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source addresses toxicity to cats or dogs; the NC State page for Olea europaea has no poisonous-plant section at all. (Search hits for 'Russian olive' are Elaeagnus, a different genus, and were ignored.)

humidity_need left null: no live admissible page states a humidity requirement. NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden describe a preference for hot/dry summers and mild/wet winters (Mediterranean climate), but that is a climate/rainfall statement, not an air-humidity value. A UF/IFAS IPM publication (IN1251) that described olives as native to 'warm, arid environments' is now retired from Ask IFAS and was not cited.

day/night temperature ranges left null: no source gives growing-season day or night ranges. The only temperature numbers found are the winter rest range of 40-50 F for two months (NC State, MBG), the 12 F survival floor and 28 F green-fruit damage point (UF/IFAS EP515), and RHS's H4 hardiness rating.

chill_damage_f = 28 is UF/IFAS's damage-onset figure for GREEN FRUIT specifically ('green fruits may be damaged at about 28°F'); ripe fruit withstands somewhat lower temperatures and the tree itself is grown where winters do not drop below 12 F (the survival floor, deliberately not used per the freeze-vs-damage rule). RHS adds, without a number, that branches can be damaged by severe frosts and that pot-grown plants should be stored frost-free and not moved outside until all danger of frost has passed.

is_houseplant = true is qualified: Missouri Botanical Garden explicitly says growing olives as houseplants or in containers brought indoors for winter 'can be difficult' and wants indoor overwintering in cool 40-50 F conditions (greenhouse/conservatory-like), not a warm living room; NC State tags it as a container and conservatory plant that can be brought indoors in colder areas. Outdoors it is a zone 8-10 tree (NC State, MBG), with some cultivars rated for 7a/7b (NC State).

light_fc values and direct_sun_hours_max left null: no foot-candle figures exist in admissible sources. NC State defines its Full sun tag as 6 or more hours of direct sun per day (a minimum, not a maximum); RHS wants 'full light' under glass.

soil_drainage = fast: RHS wants 'sharply-drained' soil and gritty loam-based compost with added sharp sand; UF/IFAS says sand-dominated soils are best because olives get root rot in moist or wet soils; NC State and MBG call it drought tolerant once established. Caveat: NC State's structured Soil Drainage tags list both 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist' (which mechanically would suggest moisture_retentive), and MBG lists Water: Medium / 'medium moisture' - the qualitative disease-risk and sharp-drainage statements were weighed over the mechanical tag.

soil_base = standard_potting is the closest enum to RHS's actual specification: peat-free John Innes No 3 (a loam-based potting compost) with added sharp sand, or 'gritty, loam-based compost' in 30-35 cm pots; add grit/sharp sand to a standard mix.

soil_ph 6.0-7.0 is the UF/IFAS olive nutrition guide's recommended target ('Keep soil pH 6.0–7.0.'). Tolerance is wider: UF/IFAS EP515 says olives grow well on almost any well-drained soil up to a pH of 8.5, NC State tags acid (<6.0), neutral and alkaline (>8.0), and RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral.

water_regime = keep_moist reflects only RHS's container advice for the GROWING SEASON ('keep the compost moist'). records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source addresses toxicity to cats or dogs. NC State notes only that hairs on the fruit may cause throat irritation and that the fruit contains the enzyme actinidin, which can also cause irritation (human context); UGA mentions cats may damage young plants, which is plant damage, not animal toxicity.
records.cool_rest_note: Deciduous vine that is hardy while dormant in winter: UGA says it is cold hardy to winter temperatures of 10 degrees Fahrenheit and suits USDA zones 7-9 (NC State 7a-9b; Missouri Botanical Garden 8-9). Young vines and spring shoots are very frost tender, and early-fall or late-spring freezes can damage or kill young vines to the ground.
unknowns: Dioecious: separate male and female plants are required for fruit (NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS, UGA). Fruit is borne only on female vines; male plants flower but bear no fruit. UGA: one male can pollinate up to eight females (commercial practice is one male per eight female vines). RHS: self-fertile cultivars exist (e.g. Actinidia deliciosa 'Jenny'), and a female such as 'Hayward' needs a male like 'Tormuri' or a self-fertile plant nearby.

toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source states toxicity or safety for cats or dogs. UGA B992's only cat mention is that cats may damage young plants (plant damage, not animal poisoning), and NC State's irritation notes (fruit hairs, actinidin enzyme) are human-oriented.

chill_damage_f left null: UGA's 10 degrees F figure is a midwinter survival/withstand threshold ('cold hardy to', 'withstanding temperatures to 10 °F'), not a damage-onset temperature, and rule 8 forbids conflating them. Sources say young shoots are damaged by spring frost and young vines can be killed to the ground by early-fall or late-spring freezes, but no damage-onset number is stated.

soil_drainage left null: every source wants free drainage (NC State tag 'Good Drainage'; UGA sandy loam or sandy clay loam with good internal drainage, raised beds where drainage is marginal, root rot when soils are too wet; RHS well-drained), yet UGA also says mature plants require consistently moist soil and calls kiwifruit the most drought-sensitive fruit in Georgia while also one of the most sensitive to overwatering. Neither 'fast' (drought-intolerant) nor 'moisture_retentive' (root-rot risk when wet) fits, and no source's structured tags span both occasionally dry and occasionally wet for 'moderate'.

Watering intervals left null: UGA says 'Water multiple times a week when the plant is young' and to water immediately if leaves fold or wilt, with no literal day count; RHS says newly planted vines need watering through the growing season for the first few years, and established plants should not need regular watering except during prolonged dry spells while fruit is swelling.

fertilize_interval_days and fertilize_strength left null: UGA gives a per-plant application rate, not a dilution — 4 oz of 10-10-10 in March, May and July the first year, scattered over a 24-inch circle, rising to 8 oz in year two, 1 lb in year three and 2 lb per application from year four once the trellis is filled. RHS says plants in regularly mulched soil should not need routine feeding; apply a granular fertiliser in early spring only if harvests are poor or a nutrient deficiency shows.

Soil pH: the 6.0-6.5 range is UGA B992's pre-planting recommendation. RHS's grow guide says 'slightly acidic' but its plant profile tags pH as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so the RHS tolerance is broader than the UGA target.

Climate limits: Penn State says fuzzy kiwi cannot be grown in Pennsylvania because of cold tenderness and a long growing season; Missouri Botanical Garden says it cannot be grown successfully in St. Louis because it is only winter hardy to Zone 8; RHS says fruit rarely ripens fully outdoors in the UK except in long hot summers — pick unripe fruit before the first hard frost and ripen indoors, which can take several weeks. Plants usually start fruiting three or four years after planting (RHS).

Site and support: protect from strong wind (NC State, UGA, RHS 'wind scorch'); plant in a warm, sheltered, sunny spot, ideally against a south- or west-facing wall (RHS); NC State says the plant does not like its roots disturbed once situated. It needs a large, sturdy trellis, pergola or T-bar trellis, spaced roughly 10-15 ft apart, and RHS recommends pruning twice a year (summer and winter).

Pests and diseases: UGA says root-knot nematodes are widespread and very destructive to kiwifruit, and warns against peanut hulls or peanut straw as mulch because peanut litter carries a destructive root disease; RHS lists honey fungus and Phytophthora root rot as possible problems. Otherwise NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden report no serious insect or disease problems.

No admissible source gives numeric day/night temperatures, humidity, foot-candle light levels, a maximum direct-sun figure, or a chill-hour requirement, so those fields are null. NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' is a minimum, not a maximum.

Source coverage: Clemson HGIC has only a photo Q&A (noting several extremely cold-hardy varieties exist and fruit in SC most years); UF/IFAS Ask IFAS/EDIS has no kiwi-growing publication (only nutrition and pest tables); UMD Extension covers hardy kiwi (Actinidia arguta) and mentions A. deliciosa only as the supermarket fruit. Nothing from those domains was usable for care fields.

records.name_note: Clemson's dedicated Blackberry factsheet and Missouri Botanical Garden's cultivar entries file cultivated blackberry under Rubus fruticosus. RHS treats the name as an aggregate, listing cultivars as "Rubus fruticosus agg.". UF/IFAS files cultivated blackberry only at genus level as Rubus spp. NC State's Plant Toolbox covers blackberry at genus level (Rubus) and through the native species Rubus allegheniensis (Allegheny Blackberry) rather than under R. fruticosus.
records.cool_rest_note: Deciduous, winter-dormant bramble: primocanes go dormant in autumn, and current cultivars need 300 to 900 chill hours below 45°F to break bud properly; inadequate chill gives poor, erratic bud break, so match the cultivar's chill-hour requirement to your climate (e.g., 'Sweet-Ark Caddo' is a 300-hour low-chill cultivar). Thornless types are more cold-sensitive, and winter injury tends to occur during fluctuating temperatures rather than in deep dormancy.
records.water_dry_down_target: Keep the root zone evenly moist but never waterlogged; the plant is intolerant of wet soils. Established in-ground plants are drought-tolerant, but do not let them dry out during establishment or while fruit is sizing and ripening.
records.water_estimate_basis: Clemson gives about 1 inch of water per week by irrigation when rainfall falls short, and Penn State 1 to 2 inches per week for home-garden brambles, so 7 days is taken as the growing-season check cadence. UMD separately notes home gardeners can substitute hand-watering several times per week for an irrigation system -- a general site-selection note, not a first-year schedule -- which implies a shorter-than-weekly check on light soils or in hot weather. In-ground guidance; a container plant dries faster.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail: left null. No admissible source addresses cat or dog toxicity for blackberry in either direction. The Clemson factsheet, Missouri Botanical Garden entry, RHS guide, UF/IFAS, UGA, UMD, and Penn State pages contain no toxicity statement at all; silence is not evidence of safety.

chill_damage_f: left null. No admissible source states a damage-onset temperature. Penn State only says thornless types are more cold sensitive and that injury often occurs during fluctuating temperatures; Missouri Botanical Garden gives 'Zone: 5 to 8' for 'Chester', a survival zone rather than a damage-onset figure; UF/IFAS says Florida plants rarely suffer winter injury.

day_f_min / day_f_max / night_f_min / night_f_max, humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max, light_fc_min / light_fc_good, direct_sun_hours_max: not addressed by any admissible source for this outdoor garden bramble. UGA's 'at least six to eight hours of sunlight' and NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours)' are minimums, not maximums.

soil_drainage: left null. Every source wants good drainage and no wet feet (Missouri Botanical Garden: 'well-drained soil ... Intolerant of wet soils'; RHS: 'good drainage. Avoid planting in areas that are likely to become waterlogged'; Penn State: not in poorly drained soils; UMD: clay soils' water holding enables Phytophthora root rot), yet the same sources also ask for moist, organically rich soil (Missouri Botanical Garden 'moist'; RHS 'Loch Ness' profile 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained') and Clemson calls the plant drought-tolerant. That 'moist but well-drained, dry-tolerant, wet-intolerant' profile does not map onto fast, moderate (which needs occasional-wet tolerance), or moisture_retentive (which needs no dry counterpart), so no enum was forced.

outdoor_sun_exposure: full_sun is unanimous. part_shade is included because the two dedicated Rubus fruticosus pages support it (Missouri Botanical Garden 'Full sun to part shade'; RHS 'will fruit in light shade'), but Clemson explicitly disagrees ('Blackberries should not be planted in part-shade to shaded areas as they will harbor more diseases and never produce good yields'), and UGA, UMD, and Penn State all frame full sun as the requirement for production. Treat part shade as tolerated with reduced yield and higher disease pressure, not as a recommendation.

soil_ph: 6.0-6.5 is the ideal range stated by Clemson, UGA, and UMD. UMD adds that plants can be grown at pH 5.5-7 but 'will not flourish if planted into low pH soils'; Missouri Botanical Garden says 'slightly acidic'. Not treated as a conflict.

water_check_depth_cm: left null. UGA's 'Apply enough water to wet the soil at least 8 to 10 inches below the ground surface' is an irrigation wetting depth (about 20-25 cm), not a moisture-check depth, so it was not mapped.

water_dormant_days_est: left null. The plant is deciduous and dormant in winter; RHS says well-established plants shouldn't need extra watering, UGA says to water during dry parts of the season, and no source gives a dormant-season interval.

water_growing_days_est = 7 is a direct reading of the sources' 'per week' irrigation guidance (Clemson 1 inch/week; Penn State 1-2 inches/week) rather than a derived interval; Penn State's figure is stated for brambles generally in a home-garden bramble article that covers blackberries, and Clemson's is blackberry-specific.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_strength: left null. All sources describe two applications per year timed to growth stage (Clemson: early spring when growth starts and again just after harvest; UGA: February or early March and June for established plants, April and July in year one; UMD: at bud break and again in May around flowering) with granular or per-acre rates (UGA 1 lb 10-10-10 per 9 ft of row then 1 lb per 18 ft; Penn State no more than 5 lb 10-10-10 per 100 ft of row in year one and 10 lb thereafter; UMD 30/45/60 lb N per acre in years 1/2/3+), not a day interval or a dilution strength. RHS says plants in regularly mulched soil shouldn't need feeding at all.

fertilize_active_months [2-7] is the union of the literal months named across regional sources (UGA Georgia: February/early March, April, June, July; UMD Mid-Atlantic: May). It is a window for two split applications, not a monthly feeding schedule, and the window shifts later in colder regions.

Catalog cross-check: this catalog already carries a record with common_name 'Blackberry' under Rubus allegheniensis (b12-fruit-and-flowers1.json) and Red Raspberry under Rubus idaeus (b27-bulbs-and-more.json). This record is the cultivated blackberry (Rubus fruticosus) companion; the duplicate common name against the R. allegheniensis record should be disambiguated at ingest (e.g., 'Allegheny Blackberry' for that record). No values here were taken from the R. idaeus or R. allegheniensis pages: NC State's R. allegheniensis and genus pages are cited only for the naming situation, and every care value is cited to a blackberry-specific statement or to a bramble statement that explicitly names blackberries.

Source availability: UF/IFAS HS104 'The Blackberry' returns HTTP 410 Gone (both edis.ifas.ufl.edu and ask.ifas.ufl.edu), so UF/IFAS coverage here comes from HS1352 'Choosing the Right Blackberry Cultivar in Subtropical Florida'. plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/rubus-fruticosus/ returns 404. The older RHS URL /fruit/blackberries/grow-your-own returns 404; the live guide is /fruit/blackberries-and-hybrid-berries/grow-your-own. www.missouribotanicalgarden.org Plant Finder URLs 301-redirect to plantfinder.mobot.org, which is the URL cited.

Cultivar dependence: chill-hour needs span 300-900 hours (UF/IFAS), thornless cultivars are more cold-sensitive (Penn State), and growth habit (trailing, semi-erect, erect) and fruiting type (floricane vs primocane) change pruning and trellis needs; all sources recommend a trellis even for erect types.

Container growing: RHS says a few compact varieties (e.g., 'Little Black Prince') can be grown in a pot at least 45 cm wide and deep in loam-based compost kept slightly moist; this record's soil_base reflects the default in-ground planting every source assumes.

water_estimate_basis — removed on audit: The clause "UMD says home gardeners should be able to water several times per week in the establishment year" (and the matching citation label "...in the establishment year") misattributes scope. On the live UMD FS-2023-0660 page the sentence sits under 'Growing site selection' immediately after the full-sun sentence and reads, with its actual context: "Commercial producers will generally use drip or overhead irrigation systems for their plants. However, for home gardeners this is not a necessary investment as long as you are able to water your plants several times per week." It is not scoped to first-year plants; it is a general site-selection note about not needing an irrigation system if you can hand-water several times a week. The factsheet as a whole is framed as first-year planting advice, but the sentence itself carries no establishment-year qualifier. Repair: drop 'in the establishment year' from both the prose and the citation label, and state it as UMD's general note that home gardeners can substitute hand-watering several times per week for an irrigation system - which also honestly records that one source implies a shorter-than-weekly cadence.

records.name_note: NC State also lists Lucky Heart Plant and Wax Hearts as common names. Penn State calls the species heart-leaf hoya and reserves 'sweetheart hoya' for the marketed single leaf, which will stay as it is and not develop into a vine; NC State and Clemson note it is sold around Valentine's Day.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State tags this species non-toxic for cats, non-toxic for dogs and non-toxic for horses.
records.cool_rest_note: No cool rest is described. NC State says temperatures below its 65-80 F ideal slow growth and flowering; RHS says to keep it just moist in winter rather than rest it cold.
records.water_dry_down_target: Let the surface of the mix dry and the pot dry somewhat between waterings, using room-temperature water; thinning, brown or wrinkled leaves mean it has been left dry too long.
unknowns: Single-leaf warning (decision-relevant, no schema field): NC State says it is often sold as a single rooted leaf that is not likely to grow well unless stem tissue was included; Penn State says the marketed 'sweetheart hoya' single leaf will stay as it is and not develop into a vine. Buyers wanting a vine should look for a stem cutting or node, not a lone leaf.

humidity_need / humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: two admissible sources disagree, so left null. UGA B-1318 Table 3 codes Hoya kerrii H=2, 'Average: 25% to 49%'; NC State's species page says it 'needs warm and humid locations' and benefits from a humid room such as a kitchen or bathroom. Treat 25-49% as the floor and extra humidity as a benefit rather than a requirement.

chill_damage_f: no source publishes an injury temperature. NC State says lower temperatures (below 65-80 F) slow growth and flowering, which is a performance floor, not damage; the RHS H1C hardiness rating (5-10 C minimum class) is a hardiness category, not an injury onset; the NC State genus page calls hoyas frost intolerant.

day/night temperatures: NC State's 65-80 F ideal range is not split by day and night, so it fills both pairs. UGA's T=2 code ('Average: 65°F night, 75°F day') corroborates the 65 F night floor and sits inside the range.

light_fc_min 200 is the floor of UGA's L=2 'High-light areas: Over 200 ft-c, but not direct sun' class assigned specifically to Hoya kerrii; no source gives a preferred (good) foot-candle figure, so light_fc_good is null.

direct_sun_hours_max: sources conflict, so null. UGA's class says not direct sun and RHS says shade from hot sun, while Clemson says hoyas near a south window must be acclimated to direct sunlight to avoid leaf burn, and RHS's structured Position field lists full sun.

outdoor_sun_exposure: RHS's structured Position tag also lists 'Full sun', but its own cultivation text says bright indirect light with shade from hot sun, NC State's genus page says hoyas do not need full sun all day, and Clemson says to summer them outdoors in a shaded area; full_sun is therefore omitted. Clemson gives above 60 F as the outdoor season.

soil_base standard_potting encodes Clemson's 'amend a standard potting mix with orchid bark and perlite' (1 part potting soil, 1 part orchid bark, 1 part perlite), RHS's fast-draining loam-based compost with extra organic matter, and UGA's S=2 foliage-plant mix (2 parts peat moss, 1 part perlite, 1 part fir bark). The amended chunky version is what all three actually recommend; NC State's structured tag gives the soil texture as Sand.

water_regime dry_surface_between follows UGA's W=2 code ('Surface of soil mix should dry before re-watering') and NC State's 'dry somewhat between watering'. Clemson's genus factsheet goes further ('dry out completely between waterings') and NC State warns that drying too much causes thin, brown or wrinkled leaves and that overwatering causes root rot and inhibits flowering. Err on the drier side of surface-dry; Clemson suggests the pot weight test.

water_check_depth_cm / water_growing_days_est / water_dormant_days_est / water_estimate_basis: no source publishes a depth or a day interval. RHS says water moderately in growth and keep just moist in winter, so watering should drop in winter.

fertilize_interval_days / fertilize_active_months / fertilize_strength: RHS says apply a balanced liquid feed monthly while in growth, but no source states a numeric interval, months or dilution, so nothing is encoded. Clemson suggests a liquid fertilizer with an NPK ratio of 2:1:2 or 3:1:2 to support flowering.

Bloom and handling cautions not captured by schema fields: NC State says the long bare twining stems should not be cut back because they precede new leaves and flowers; flowers drip copious reddish-brown nectar that stains fabrics, walls and furnishings; the plant is shy to flower when young and RHS gives 5-10 years to maturity; RHS says hoyas resent repotting and can stay in the same pot for many years; Penn State says not to move or rotate a plant once a flower begins to form.

records.name_note: Also widely called Northern Pitcher Plant; the RHS and Missouri Botanical Garden single-species pages lead with the name "common pitcher plant".
records.cool_rest_note: Needs a true cold winter dormancy, not merely a rest. NC State: it goes dormant in fall and stays dormant until spring (leave browned foliage until just before flowers emerge). Missouri Botanical Garden: it needs cold temperatures for winter dormancy, which is why it often does not grow well as a houseplant. RHS: in winter keep it slightly drier, cool and well ventilated; it loses some leaves during dormancy. Penn State: overwinter containers in an unheated garage, cold frame or protected outdoor site. Clemson's generic guideline for temperate carnivorous plants is at least 45 days below 45 degrees F. The plant is frost-hardy outdoors (RHS: hardy to around -15 C, rating H6; NC State: USDA zones 4a-9b; MBG: zones 3-8) but must be protected from freezing winds.
records.water_dry_down_target: Never let the medium dry out. Keep it constantly damp/moist through the growing season (stand the container in a tray or saucer of low-mineral water; RHS cites 2.5-5 cm), but do not let the crown sit in water and do not keep the plant sodden. In winter keep it only slightly drier: compost damp rather than wet, watering when it is just starting to dry out and discarding excess.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source addresses cats or dogs. The NC State species page has no poison section and the RHS species page lists no 'potentially harmful' entry; absence of a warning is not evidence of safety.

Fertilizer: all fertilize_* fields are deliberately null because the sources say do not fertilize. NC State: 'fertilizers can burn the plant'; Missouri Botanical Garden: 'Do not fertilize plantings' and 'Potting soil and/or fertilizer may kill the plant'; RHS: needs no additional fertiliser and will die if given any kind of fertiliser; Clemson: 'Do not fertilize'. Do not hand-feed with food scraps either (NC State, MBG).

Water quality is a hard requirement: use rainwater, distilled, reverse-osmosis or other lime-free/demineralized water. NC State says it is sensitive to dissolved salts in chlorinated water; RHS says tap-water chemicals, especially in hard-water areas, can be toxic to it; Penn State waters with distilled water; Clemson says always use demineralized water.

soil_base left null: no enum token matches. Sources call for a low-nutrient, acidic mix of peat (or sustainably sourced sphagnum) with sand or perlite (MBG: 50% peat / 50% perlite or vermiculite; NC State: sand and peat, mostly sand; Penn State: 1 part peat to 1 part silica sand or chicken grit; Clemson: half sphagnum peat and half perlite or play sand). Ordinary potting soil or garden soil is explicitly warned against (MBG: may kill the plant; RHS: never plant in soil or potting compost).
soil_ph_min left null: sources say only 'acid'/'acidic'; NC State's 'Acid (<6.0)' supplies the maximum only.

chill_damage_f left null: sources give freeze-survival/hardiness figures (RHS: hardy to around -15 C, H6 = -20 to -15 C; NC State: USDA zones 4a-9b and hardy to zone 3 in the north of its range; MBG: zones 3-8), not a damage-onset temperature. The plant requires cold winter dormancy; the only stated cold hazard is freezing wind (NC State, MBG).
Growing-season temperature ranges (day_f_*, night_f_*) left null: no admissible source states them.

humidity_need left null: the only humidity statement is Clemson's generic indoor carnivorous-terrarium guidance 'Moderate to high with adequate airflow', which is group-level rather than species-specific and spans two enum tokens.

Light: no foot-candle figures in any source. Outdoors it wants full sun (NC State: 6 or more hours direct sun; MBG: in part shade colour fails to develop and pitchers droop). Indoors/under glass, RHS advises full light but shelter from hot sun and a bright position not usually in direct sun because leaves can scorch through glass; Clemson's terrarium guide uses 12 to 14 hours of direct full-spectrum artificial light per day.

Watering intervals (water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est) left null: no source gives a numeric cadence. Method is tray/saucer watering in the growing season (RHS: saucer up to 2.5 cm for houseplants, 2.5-5 cm generally; MBG: tray of water keeping soil constantly moist), Penn State: 'water regularly with distilled water when rain is not consistent', and in winter RHS says water only when the compost is starting to dry out and discard the excess.

Houseplant caveat: RHS calls it relatively easy to grow as a houseplant and tags the species page 'Houseplants', but Missouri Botanical Garden says it often does not grow well as a houseplant because it needs growing-season sun and cold winter dormancy, and NC State says indoors it requires sun for the growing season and then winter dormancy. Plan for a cold, bright rest period if kept indoors.

Overwatering nuance: despite wanting constantly moist soil, NC State says 'The biggest mistake is keeping the plant too wet' and MBG says crowns should not sit in water; root rot is listed as a problem by both.
Never collect from the wild: NC State, MBG, UF/IFAS and Clemson all say to buy nursery-grown plants only; wild populations are threatened and poaching is illegal.

Naming: UF/IFAS lists the Gulf Coast population under 'Gulf Purple Pitcherplant' with Sarracenia rosea as a synonym and 'Decumbent pitcherplant, northern pitcherplant' as other names; MBG and RHS recognise subsp. purpurea (northern) and subsp. venosa (southern), which hybridise where ranges overlap.
Penn State says pitcher plants can be grown outdoors in containers in hardiness zones 5 and 6 with the containers overwintered in an unheated garage, cold frame or protected outdoor site.

records.name_note: The species-level common name is "Winged Tropical Pitcher Plant" (RHS dedicated single-species profile; NC State cultivar entry). "Tropical Pitcher Plant" is the genus-level common name that NC State and Clemson apply to Nepenthes generally, not to this species alone.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State tags Nepenthes non-toxic for cats and non-toxic for dogs; Clemson's Nepenthes spp. factsheet lists "Pet Safe: Yes". No admissible source reports any cat or dog toxicity for this species.
records.cool_rest_note: No cool winter rest is described by any admissible source. RHS rates Nepenthes alata H1A, meaning it is kept under glass all year at above 15C (59F); the cool nights mentioned for highland Nepenthes are a daily day-night drop, not a seasonal rest.
records.water_dry_down_target: None: keep the medium continuously moist and never let the plant dry out, using rainwater or distilled water rather than tap water.
unknowns: Source scope: the only admissible page dedicated solely to Nepenthes alata is the RHS Plant Profile. The NC State Plant Toolbox page and the Clemson HGIC 1571 factsheet are genus-level (Nepenthes / Nepenthes spp.) but both name Nepenthes alata explicitly as a recommended, easy-to-grow species; genus-level care values from those two pages are used only where the species is within their stated scope.

No Sarracenia content was used. The UF/IFAS 'Native Pitcherplants of Florida' (WEC333/UW378) publication and the Penn State 'Carnivorous Plants' article both cover Sarracenia and other temperate bog carnivores only, never Nepenthes, and were excluded. MoBot PlantFinder, UMD Extension and UGA field reports returned no Nepenthes page.

Water quality is critical: NC State says carnivorous plants cannot tolerate watering with tap water and that distilled water or rainwater should be used; Clemson says plants can be sensitive to tap water and to use rainwater or distilled water; the RHS carnivorous-plant guide says to use rainwater whenever possible.

Fertilizer cautions (carnivorous plant): feeding is optional and only if insects are not provided. Clemson says an organic fertilizer (fish emulsion, seaweed or kelp extract) can be applied 'twice a month during the growing season', diluted to about quarter strength and applied to the leaves and open pitchers, not the root medium. NC State says an organic fertilizer may be used during the growing season if insects are unavailable, and that the plants do not digest protein and should not be fed meat. The RHS guide states most carnivorous plants need no additional fertiliser. fertilize_interval_days is left null because 'twice a month' is a word cadence, not a literal day count; fertilize_active_months is null because no source lists calendar months.

fertilize_strength: the Clemson dilution sentence reads verbatim 'Dilute the fertilizer to ¼ to of the recommended strength.' and appears to have a dropped upper fraction after 'to'; only the quarter-strength figure is legible, so 'quarter' is recorded.

chill_damage_f and night_f_min both come from Clemson's species-specific statement that Nepenthes alata tolerates 54F to 95F; the source frames 54F as the floor of a tolerance range rather than an explicit damage-onset temperature. RHS's H1A rating (kept under glass all year above 15C / 59F) is a more conservative year-round minimum.

Neither source assigns Nepenthes alata to the lowland or highland group; Clemson describes it only as 'a widespread species that grows in the hills surrounding jungles'. day_f_min 70 is the daytime floor shared by both groups in Clemson (lowland 70-95F; highland 70-80F), and day_f_max 95 is both the lowland maximum and the species' stated upper tolerance. night_f_max is null because no source gives a night maximum for this species or for lowland Nepenthes (lowland nights are described only as 'warm').

Light: no admissible source gives foot-candle values, so light_fc_min and light_fc_good are null. direct_sun_hours_max 6 is the upper bound of NC State's Partial Shade tag (2-6 hours); Clemson says only 'a few hours of direct sun in the morning or late afternoon' and RHS says bright filtered light, so treat 6 hours as an upper limit rather than a target.

Soil: soil_base 'orchid_bark' is the closest enum to the sources' actual recommendation, which is a sphagnum-dominant, low-nutrient mix (Clemson: 60% sphagnum moss, 20% perlite, 20% orchid bark; NC State: sphagnum moss or orchid mix with peat and perlite; RHS: acidic, low-nutrient specialist mix). NC State says garden soil is not tolerated as a potting medium, and the RHS guide says never to plant carnivorous plants in soil or potting compost. soil_ph_min is null; sources say only 'acid' / 'Acid (<6.0)'.

Watering interval: no admissible source gives a numeric watering interval; the regime is keep-moist with no dry-down, so water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis and water_check_depth_cm are null.
Pitcher failure and die-back are attributed to low humidity and low light (Clemson; NC State), which is why humidity_need is high with a 60% floor; no source gives an upper humidity bound.
Clemson warns to avoid copper-based fungicides, as they can kill tropical pitcher plants.

Common-name choice: the task label 'Tropical Pitcher Plant' is the genus-level name; per the naming rule the record uses the name led by the dedicated single-species page (RHS: 'winged tropical pitcher plant'), which NC State's species entry also uses.

records.cool_rest_note: Plants go dormant if exposed to temperatures consistently below 40°F, but a cool rest is optional: MOBOT says it can be grown indoors with or without a dormancy period and kept in continuous growth in a warm, humid environment with supplemental light.

unknowns: fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months and fertilize_strength are deliberately null: this is a carnivorous plant. NC State's Drosera page says 'Do not apply fertilizers' and Clemson's carnivorous-plant factsheet says these plants can be damaged by fertilizer; neither dedicated species page mentions feeding. Do not fertilize.

Water quality matters more than schedule: MOBOT says to water with rain water or deionized water, RHS keeps the pot standing in a saucer of rainwater, and NC State says to always use rainwater or distilled water. Avoid tap or mineral-rich water.

soil_base is null because no enum token fits: MOBOT prescribes a sphagnum-based potting soil with plenty of sand and/or perlite (unfertilized), while RHS tags 'Loam' but its cultivation text calls for wet, acidic bog conditions. A fertilized commercial potting or ericaceous mix would be inappropriate.

soil_drainage = moisture_retentive reflects a constantly wet root zone in both sources (MOBOT: consistently moist, Water: Wet, Tolerate: Wet Soil; RHS: Poorly-drained). MOBOT also calls the mix 'well-draining' - the sand/perlite gives an open structure, but it is never allowed to dry out.
soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max are null: RHS gives only 'Acid or Neutral' and 'wet, acidic conditions' with no numeric range.
water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est and water_estimate_basis are null: no source states an interval; the regime is tray/saucer watering with no dry-down target.

chill_damage_f is null: no source states a damage-onset temperature. MOBOT gives dormancy onset at temperatures consistently below 40°F and hardiness in USDA Zones 7 to 9; RHS rates it H3 (hardy in coastal and relatively mild parts of the UK, -5 to 1 C). These are dormancy and survival thresholds, not damage onset.
day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max are null: no source gives numeric growing temperatures; MOBOT only says 'warm' for indoor continuous growth.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good and direct_sun_hours_max are null: no source gives foot-candles or hours. Both species pages call for full sun outdoors; RHS says under glass to give full light but shade from hot sun; MOBOT says indoor growth needs supplemental light.
humidity_pct_min/max are null: MOBOT calls for a 'warm, humid' indoor environment without a percentage; humidity_need = high is taken from that wording.
toxic_to_pets is null: no admissible source addresses Drosera capensis toxicity to cats or dogs, and sundews do not appear on the extension pet-toxicity lists searched (Clemson, UGA, UMD).
MOBOT rates maintenance High. Mature plants reach up to about 6 inches tall (RHS: 0.1-0.5 m); MOBOT's header line 'Height: 2.50 to 6.00 feet' conflicts with its own description and with RHS.
RHS propagation: seed, softwood cuttings, or root cuttings taken when dormant.
